section.title: Conservation laws in one dimension
section.p: The last section rewrote the Fundamental Theorem as a boundary theorem:
The interval contributes its two endpoints. The inside contributes a derivative. The same boundary idea explains one of the most important patterns in science:
section.md: \text{what is inside changes because something crosses the boundary or is created inside.}
section.p: That sentence is a conservation law.

exercise.title: Why are density and flux different quantities?

statement.p: Density \rho measures how much is present per unit length. Flux q measures how fast stuff crosses a point. In your own words, why can a traffic jam have high density and small flux, and why do you need both quantities to write a conservation law?

hint.p: Being crowded is not the same as moving. Conservation tracks how the amount inside changes, which requires both how much is there and how much is crossing the ends.

subsection.p: The signs contain the orientation. Positive flux points to the right. At the left endpoint, rightward flux enters the interval. At the right endpoint, rightward flux leaves the interval.

exercise.title: Why is the rate of change inside equal to inflow minus outflow?

statement.p: With no sources or sinks, \frac{d}{dt}\int_a^b \rho\,dx=q(a,t)-q(b,t). In your own words, why do the signs match the orientation of the interval, and why is this the same boundary idea as the Fundamental Theorem?

hint.p: Positive flux points to the right, so it enters at the left endpoint and leaves at the right. The interior changes because of what happens on the signed boundary.

warning.title: Warning
warning.p: Boundary flux alone explains the change inside only when there are no sources or sinks inside the interval.
If material is created or destroyed inside, the source term must be included.

paragraphs.p: This is the same kind of honesty we used throughout calculus. A theorem’s hypotheses are not decoration. They say exactly what the formula is allowed to ignore.

exercise.title: Why must sources and sinks be named separately?

statement.p: Boundary flux alone explains the change inside only when nothing is created or destroyed in the interval. In your own words, why is that hypothesis part of the conservation law, and how does a source term restore honesty when cars appear from an on-ramp?

hint.p: A theorem cannot ignore what it has not been told about. If material is created inside, the accounting must include an interior integral of the source rate.

subsection.p: In multivariable calculus, the flux becomes a vector field. Instead of moving only left or right, material can flow in many directions. The derivative q_x becomes divergence:

The idea is the same as the one-dimensional version:
This is why the boundary viewpoint matters. The Fundamental Theorem, flux through endpoints, conservation laws, and divergence are not separate tricks. They are stages of one story:

There is one final bridge. Calculus has optimized numbers: shortest distance, largest area, greatest profit. But physics and geometry often ask for the best path. That means optimizing a whole function.

exercise.title: Why does an interval law become a local law?

statement.p: If the conservation identity holds on every interval, the integrand \rho_t+q_x must vanish. In your own words, why does that local equation deserve the name divergence, and what does it say about how interior change is produced by nearby flux imbalance?

hint.p: An integral that vanishes on every interval forces the integrand to be zero. The term q_x measures how flux is increasing as you move along the line, which is the one-dimensional divergence.
